newsitem.title: USA: Bell Atlantic, Nynex see U.S. merger approval soon.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic, Nynex see U.S. merger approval soon.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp. and Nynex Corp. predicted Thursday their merger would soon win Justice Department clearance, the last big hurdle for the $23 billion deal announced a year ago.
The merger, if approved, would create the second-largest U.S. telecommunications company, behind only long-distance giant AT&T Corp.

"We still expect the merger to be approved promptly (by the Department of Justice)," said a spokesman for Philadelphia-based Bell Atlantic. A spokesman for New York-based Nynex concurred. But antitrust experts are divided over whether approval is a sure bet.
A source familiar with the case said a decision by the department's antitrust division is expected some time this month and could come very soon.

At the very least, antitrust enforcers are expected to impose conditions on the marriage to ensure that potential competitors are not shut out of the new Bell's operating turf, which would extend from Maine to Virginia.

"This is a troublesome and novel case. Hence, it's hard to predict exactly how it's going to come out," said Donald Baker, an attorney with Baker & Miller who headed the antitrust division in the early 1980s during the breakup of the old Ma Bell.

New York regulators approved the Bell Atlantic-Nynex merger last month after imposing conditions, such as getting assurances that the new carrier's headquarters would be in New York and that the company would hire more employees.
The Justice Department decision is expected to influence the Federal Communications Commission, which also must sign off on the transaction.

The new Bell Atlantic would rank 23rd on Fortune magazine's list of the 500 largest U.S. corporations. It would operate about 40 million phone lines around the globe, with combined revenues of nearly $30 billion.
Antitrust officials must decide whether the merger would hurt competition. But officials are faced with two companies that do not yet operate in the same geographical areas.
"I'd be awfully surprised if it gets challenged," said attorney Joe Sims of Jones, Day, Reavis & Pogue. "Potential competition cases are very hard."
To block the deal, Justice Department officials would have to use the relatively untried argument that potential competition would be harmed.

That would hinge on trying to prove that if the merger had not taken place, Bell Atlantic would have expanded to offer services in New York City -- a suggestion that Bell Atlantic officials have always denied.

"The notion that you're going to stop a merger that doesn't eliminate existing competition but might eliminate competition that might exist in the future -- you've got a lot of mights there," said Sims.
But Baker of Baker & Miller was more cautious. "The telephone companies still have substantial monopoly power in their local areas. So that is some sort of antitrust concern," he said.
